trajectory_summary: The call opens with the customer trying to withdraw the lead entirely, and the rep's boundary correction at 01:08 successfully reverses that and keeps the conversation alive through a full verify sequence. From there the call is mixed: qualification items get captured (roof ownership, spouse on title, utility, a bill figure, a self-reported credit score) but several are captured shallowly — the credit claim is unverified, the interest-reason answer is thin and not built on, and the bill number is never flipped into urgency. The call ends in a soft, unlocked callback with no day/time and no confirmed spouse presence.
outcome_dispute: The v1 tag is unknown/unclear; based on the transcript this should be recorded as a callback, not a booked or tentative appointment — the customer explicitly says he will call back after discussing with his spouse, and the rep never proposes or locks a day/time.

primary_coaching_focus.topic: Unanchored close / no locked callback time
primary_coaching_focus.quote: K. Yeah. That sounds good. I'll just send you a text as well. And then if you can find that bill and send me a photo of it, that'd be great.
primary_coaching_focus.why: The entire qualification effort in this call (boundary correction, roof ownership, spouse identification, bill capture, credit claim) is put at risk by an ending with zero locked time, no spouse-inclusion proposal for the next step, and no handshake — this is the single highest-leverage fix because it governs whether any of the upstream work converts into a real appointment.

key_moments.quote: Yeah. Well, we would actually we it looks like you are in our boundaries, so we'd be able to get you a system.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is actually a well-handled factual correction, not a true inversion opportunity — the customer's stated reason (told solar isn't available there) was misinformation, not a cost/time/interest objection, so a factual correction was the right tool rather than a flip. Classification here is to flag that Stewart considered and rejected the inversion frame.

The customer's stated figure is almost certainly a mis-transcription or shorthand for $250/month (a bare $2.50 electric bill is not plausible), but this is an assumed correction, not a settled fact — the transcript itself only contains '$2.50.' Whatever the true figure, the rep captured a number and moved straight to the program pitch without acknowledging or reflecting the bill back to the customer.

key_moments.quote: My credit score is the best that anyone can have.
key_moments.stewart_read: This is a stated-but-unverified and non-numeric credit claim — the customer never gives an actual number, just a vague superlative. The rep accepts it immediately with no follow-up probe for an actual score or range, directly touching the schema's open policy question about stated vs. pulled credit.

key_moments.quote: And then I'm assuming you're just wanting to save on your electric bills?
key_moments.stewart_read: Rather than asking an open interest question and letting the customer answer, the rep supplies the assumed answer for the customer. The customer then corrects him ("Not really because... we're very tight on how we use electricity consumption"), revealing the assumption was wrong and the real motivation (efficiency/curiosity about optimal usage) went uncaptured with any depth.
